newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seeks to build re-election bridge with PMDB.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seeks to build re-election bridge with PMDB.

text.p: Brazil's government on Thursday was seeking to settle differences with the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and press ahead with voting on President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election bid, officials said.

"Bridges are being rebuilt," said a government official in Congress. "The government still wants to put re-election to a first vote (on the floor of the Chamber of Deputies) in January but we don't know how easy that will be."
The government's hopes of getting re-election through the lower house in January, allowing it to revive its reform program, were dashed this week by a rebellion by the PMDB's anti-government wing.

A recommendation by a PMDB convention that party lawmakers vote on re-election only after upcoming internal congressional elections was ignored by six PMDB deputies who voted in favor of the reform in Chamber of Deputies committee on Wednesday.
But there was no sign of the PMDB taking part in the next stage of the bill's progress through Congress -- the first of two votes on the floor of the lower house.

Government whips recognize they have no chance of reaching the three-fifths majority needed in each of the those two votes without the PMDB, the largest in the Chamber of Deputies with 102 of a total 513 deputies, and the biggest in the Senate too.

Inocencio Oliveira, lower house whip of the Liberal Front Party (PFL), said the PMDB might be persuaded take part in a first vote on re-election around Jan. 29 followed by a second vote after Feb. 15. That plan could be interpreted as consistent with the convention's recommendation because final approval of re-election would only be granted after Feb. 15, he said,

Jorge Bornhausen, a former PFL president and a party heavyweight, was quoted by newspaper O Globo as suggesting the crisis could be defused if the government found a new candidate for the Senate presidency acceptable to both the PFL and PMDB.

The Senate race, due to be decided Feb. 4, is considered the root of this week's crisis. Anger among PMDB senators at what they saw as government support for a candidate from the PFL fuelled anti-government sentiment at Sunday's convention.

"Finding an alternative candidate to run the Senate appears to be the only solution but the PMDB is still in a very confrontationsl mood," said Maria Teresa Sedek, a politics professor at Sao Paulo University.

She said that while Cardoso's re-election plan had not been completely knocked off course, harsh criticism by the president of the PMDB had riled party bosses and made them less likely to want to seek a quick solution to the impasse.
Analysts from the financial sector, who see Cardoso's re-election as the best guarantee of continued economic and structural reform in Brazil, were breezy about the whole affair.

"There are going to be lots of bumps along the road...but (re-election) will ultimately go through," Larry Goodman, head of Latin American research with Salomon Brothers in New York told Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday.
Antonio Carlos Castrucce, president of the Brazilian Association of Commerical Banks, said the delay over re-election would not hurt the government's economic program.
"Reforms have been stop-and-start for the last two years. I don't see how a few more weeks are going to make much difference," Castrucce said.
